questions.stem: A teenage client presents with sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Testicular torsion is strongly suspected. Which action is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Obtain Doppler ultrasonography first and contact urology after imaging if torsion remains likely, because imaging can help distinguish causes of acute scrotal pain.","B":"Arrange immediate urologic evaluation for suspected testicular torsion, because prompt detorsion is critical and is ideally completed within 4–6 hours of pain onset.","C":"Begin empiric treatment for epididymitis while awaiting outpatient reassessment, because infection can also cause unilateral scrotal pain and tenderness in adolescents.","D":"Attempt manual detorsion and observe the response before arranging surgery, because symptom improvement can help determine whether operative exploration is needed."}}
questions.rationale: The EAU guideline identifies testicular torsion as a paediatric urologic emergency requiring immediate treatment and states that outcome is best when intervention occurs as early as possible, ideally within 4–6 hours. Option B is therefore the best action. Option A is inferior because Doppler ultrasonography is useful but should not delay intervention when torsion is strongly suspected. Option C risks a dangerous delay by treating presumed epididymitis without first resolving the torsion emergency. Option D is unsafe because manual detorsion may be attempted while awaiting surgery, but symptom improvement does not replace urgent surgical exploration and fixation.
questions.source_name: European Association of Urology — Paediatric Urology Guideline: Acute Scrotum
questions.source_detail: Current EAU Paediatric Urology guidance states that sudden severe scrotal pain with nausea/vomiting is typical of torsion, the critical window is approximately 4–6 hours, Doppler ultrasonography should not delay intervention, and urgent surgical exploration is required.

questions.stem: A client with benign prostatic hyperplasia has severe lower abdominal discomfort, has been unable to void for several hours, and has a palpable distended bladder. Which condition and response are most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Acute cystitis with secondary voiding difficulty, managed first with urine studies and antimicrobial treatment while monitoring the bladder distention.","B":"Renal colic from ureteral obstruction, managed first with analgesia and imaging because severe urinary tract pain can temporarily interfere with voiding.","C":"Acute urinary retention from bladder outlet obstruction, requiring prompt bladder decompression with catheterization while the underlying cause is evaluated.","D":"Chronic urinary retention related to BPH, managed initially with outpatient medication adjustment because a palpable bladder can occur without urgent decompression."}}
questions.rationale: Current MSD Manual guidance describes acute urinary retention as cessation of urination that can cause abdominal distention and pain; prostate abnormalities are a common cause of outlet obstruction in men, and relief of acute retention requires urethral catheterization. Option C therefore best fits the presentation and management. Option A does not explain the full painful distended-bladder retention syndrome and would delay decompression. Option B describes upper-tract obstruction and does not best account for a palpable distended bladder with complete inability to void. Option D misclassifies an acute painful inability to void as chronic retention and delays required decompression.
questions.source_name: MSD Manual Professional Edition — Urinary Retention
questions.source_detail: Full review March 2026; updated April 2026. The professional manual states that urinary retention may be acute or chronic, prostate abnormalities commonly cause outlet obstruction in men, acute retention can cause abdominal distention and pain, and relief of acute urinary retention requires urethral catheterization.

questions.stem: A client develops a severe systemic allergic-like reaction immediately after iodinated IV contrast. An IgE-mediated mechanism has not been established. Which principle should guide emergency treatment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Begin antihistamine and corticosteroid therapy while monitoring closely, and reserve epinephrine until additional findings clarify whether the reaction is IgE mediated.","B":"Manage the event as a physiologic contrast reaction with oxygen and IV fluids because lack of prior sensitization makes a severe allergic-like mechanism less likely.","C":"Stop the contrast and observe the initial response before escalating therapy, because many contrast reactions improve after exposure ends and supportive care begins.","D":"Treat the reaction according to its allergic-like severity, using epinephrine promptly when indicated for severe airway, bronchospastic, or hypotensive manifestations."}}
questions.rationale: The ACR Manual on Contrast Media 2026 states that allergic-like iodinated contrast reactions can resemble true allergic reactions even when an antigen-antibody mechanism is not identified, that prior sensitization is not required, and that treatment of an allergic-like contrast reaction is identical to that of an equivalent allergic reaction. Option D is therefore correct; the adult treatment tables include epinephrine for severe manifestations. Option A inappropriately delays epinephrine and relies on corticosteroids, which ACR states are not useful for acute treatment. Option B incorrectly reclassifies an allergic-like presentation as physiologic. Option C risks delaying indicated emergency therapy.
questions.source_name: American College of Radiology — ACR Manual on Contrast Media 2026
questions.source_detail: ACR Manual on Contrast Media 2026: allergic-like iodinated contrast reactions can occur without prior sensitization; treatment is identical to that of an equivalent allergic reaction. The adult acute-reaction tables use epinephrine for severe manifestations, and corticosteroids are not useful for acute treatment.

questions.stem: A nurse is interpreting the baseline fetal heart rate during labor. Which baseline range is considered normal in the standardized three-tier intrapartum interpretation system?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"90–110 beats/min, a range that can be accepted as a normal baseline when variability is moderate and no recurrent decelerations are present.","B":"100–170 beats/min, a range that represents the normal baseline used by the current three-tier intrapartum classification system.","C":"120–180 beats/min, a range that remains within normal limits unless persistent fetal tachycardia develops with additional tracing abnormalities.","D":"110–160 beats/min, the normal baseline range used in the current standardized intrapartum fetal heart-rate classification system."}}
questions.rationale: ACOG's fetal heart tracing definitions identify a normal baseline fetal heart rate as 110–160 beats/min and use the three-tier Category I/II/III framework. Option D is therefore correct. Option A includes values below the bradycardia threshold. Option B widens both the lower and upper limits beyond the standard range. Option C excludes normal values from 110–119 and includes values above the tachycardia threshold. Currentness was rechecked against ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10 from October 2025, which continues to use the three-tier intrapartum classification framework.
questions.source_name: ACOG — Fetal Heart Tracing Definitions; currentness checked against Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10
questions.source_detail: ACOG's fetal heart tracing definitions list a normal baseline of 110–160 beats/min and use the three-tier system. Currentness was rechecked against ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10, Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring: Interpretation and Management (October 2025).
